title: Tech stocks: how to analyze technology companies
description: Tech stocks: recurring software revenue and chip cycles demand different analysis. How to calculate ARR, margins and P/S — with examples and sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Tech stocks are shares in companies selling digital products and services — from software giants paid monthly to semiconductor equipment makers whose factories cost billions. In AK1A's hundred-company universe, technology has the highest AKM2 median (61 points out of 100) and a wide spread: 37–78, from Sinch to Logitech. One sector label hides completely different business models — so analyzing tech stocks begins not with the ratios but with one question: what kind of technology company is this?

This guide keeps the two worlds apart — software and hardware — and shows how revenue, margins and valuation are analyzed in each: the ARR calculation, the gross margin's fingerprint, the P/S ratio with the margin in mind, and the risks in cycles, competition and regulation. With worked examples and sources, as always: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are tech stocks? Two worlds to keep apart

The first world is software and digital services: companies with subscription revenue, gross margins of 70–85 percent and small capital needs — every new customer adds almost pure margin: the code is written once and sold many times. The SaaS companies belong here, but also platforms whose value grows with each new user — network effects, which build moats and sharpen the pitfall that the winner can take almost everything. The universe's technology group spans cloud communications company Sinch and consumer electronics maker Logitech; a neighboring sector adds Truecaller — the same digital business logic under another label.

The second world is hardware. Ericsson and Nokia build equipment for telecom networks; ASM International makes machines that in turn make chips. Here margins are lower, competition global and demand cyclical — the order book swings with the operators' investment budgets and the semiconductor cycle. Same label, entirely different analytical register.

Behind both worlds stands strong demand: Gartner forecasts world IT spending reaching 6.37 trillion dollars in 2026, up 14.2 percent. That number measures the sector's tailwind — not any individual company. Aggregate growth is a weather report; stock analysis is done at company level.

## Tech companies' revenue — ARR and net expansion

For a software company, the central question is how much revenue recurs by itself. The measure is ARR — annual recurring revenue — separated in the report from one-off revenue such as consulting, integration and hardware sales. A company where 90 percent of revenue is recurring is analyzed completely differently from one where every quarter starts at zero: the first has a visible revenue base, the second a sales machine restarted every period. How to read the split: [the ARR growth course](/kurser/v02-arr-tillvaxt), deeper in [our ARR walkthrough](/blogg/arr-tillvaxt-vad-atkommande-intakter-sager).

The second measure is net expansion — net revenue retention: how much revenue from existing customers grows or shrinks over twelve months, without a single new customer signed. Worked example: a company with ARR of SEK 1,000 million and net revenue retention of 110 percent has SEK 1,100 million a year later from the same customers. The SEK 100 million expansion equals winning a large new account — without acquisition cost. Below 100, a warning sounds: customers leave or shrink faster than they grow, and new sales must run just to stand still. Two controls belong beside it: how concentrated the revenue is on individual customers ([revenue diversification](/blogg/intaktsdiversifiering-risken-som-inte-syns-i-pe)) and how much of the growth is organic rather than bought.

## Margins reveal the business model

The gross margin is the technology company's fingerprint. Software with recurring revenue typically sits at 70–85 percent; hardware at 30–50; hybrids in between. The margin decides what a unit of revenue is worth: the same sales at twice the gross margin hold twice the room for development, sales and profit. Two technology companies with different gross margins should therefore never be compared on revenue alone — that is like comparing a restaurant's turnover with a licensor's. [The gross margin course](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) builds the whole sorting.

For growth companies an established rule of thumb sums up the trade-off between growth and profitability: the Rule of 40 — growth rate in percent plus EBITDA margin in percent, where a sum above 40 reads as growth worth its price tag. A company with 30 percent growth and a 12 percent EBITDA margin lands on 42; a standstill company needs a 40 percent margin for the same sum. It is a measure, not a law — but it forces you to see two numbers instead of one.

## How to value tech stocks — P/S with the margin in mind

When profit is small or negative the P/E goes quiet, and valuation moves to the revenue multiple: the P/S ratio (price divided by sales) or EV/Sales (whole-company value divided by sales). But P/S without the margin is meaningless. Two companies at the same P/S of 3 — one a software company with an 80 percent gross margin, the other a hardware company with 35 — are not comparable: the software company's cash-flow potential per unit of revenue is more than twice as high. Rule: read the revenue multiple with the gross margin, preferably also net revenue retention. The basics: [the P/S guide](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart) and [the EV course](/kurser/vm-08-evsales).

A worked example: a company with revenue of SEK 1,000 million trades at a P/S of 5 — a value of SEK 5,000 million (simplified, without debt differences). The net margin is 25 percent, the profit therefore SEK 250 million: the implicit P/E is 20. Raise the net margin to 30 percent at an unchanged price and the P/E falls to just under 17 — the multiple compresses through profitability alone, price unmoved. Growth does the same job over time: with revenue growing 20 percent per year, the P/S stands at 3.5 after two years at an unchanged price. That is why a high multiple with high growth and a high margin can be justified — and why [the PEG ratio's pitfalls](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) deserve a separate reading before trusting any single number.

## The risks — cycles, competition and regulation

- **The hardware cycle.** The semiconductor industry swings between capacity shortage and overcapacity; the order book can be full one year and empty the next. Read the cycle through [cyclically adjusted multiples](/kurser/vm-04-cyklisk-justering), never a peak year against a trough year.
- **Innovation risk.** Technology shifts — mobile, cloud, AI — can tear down a leadership position in a few years. The moat must be structural: network effects ([the course](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter)), patents and IP ([the course](/kurser/v13-patent-ip)) or high switching costs for customers.
- **Regulation.** Data is the raw material of tech companies — and their regulatory exposure. GDPR sets fines of up to 4 percent of global annual turnover or 20 million euros; the Digital Markets Act can classify large platforms as gatekeepers with obligations and fines up to 10 percent of worldwide turnover. [The data risk course](/kurser/rk-13-gdpr-och-datarisk) frames the field.
- **The balance sheet's intangibles.** Acquisition-driven growth builds goodwill that must be tested every year — [goodwill and intangible assets](/kurser/km-022-goodwill-och-immateriella-tillgangar) shows where the risk hides.
- **Cash burn.** Growth companies not yet profitable are analyzed on the cash position: burn rate, runway and the path to profitability ([cash burn](/kurser/v19-kapitalforbranning)).

## The summary

- Tech stocks are two worlds: software's recurring revenue and high margins, hardware's cycles and capital intensity — the analysis begins with which world the company lives in.
- The measures: ARR's share of revenue, net revenue retention above or below 100, the gross margin's fingerprint, the Rule of 40 as the summary.
- Valuation: P/S and EV/Sales are always read with the gross margin alongside; the worked example shows the P/E fall from 20 to just under 17 through profitability alone.
- The risks: cycles, technology shifts, regulation (GDPR, DMA), goodwill and cash burn — each visible in the accounts in advance.
